Control Valves
Control Valve Maintenance: Preventive vs Predictive Strategy, Inspection Checklist, Packing, Trim, Seat Leak Test, Bench Set and Diagnostics

A control valve wears quietly until the loop starts hunting, the packing weeps or the valve passes when closed. This page gives a field ready plan for inspection, overhaul, testing and diagnostics so the valve keeps doing its job.

Preventive vs Predictive Inspection Checklist Packing and Trim Seat Leak Test Air Leak Cost Calculator

Control valve maintenance keeps the body, trim, packing, actuator and positioner working so the valve follows its signal and shuts off tight. Learn strategies, checks, overhaul steps, seat tests, diagnostics, intervals and spares.

Hello everyone, today we are going to learn control valve maintenance, from routine inspection and packing adjustment to trim overhaul, seat leak testing and diagnostics.
Quick Answer

What is control valve maintenance and what does it include?

Control valve maintenance is the planned inspection, adjustment, repair and testing of the body, trim, packing, actuator, positioner and air supply so the valve follows its signal and meets its shut off class. For example, UNITEC D suggests monthly or quarterly visual checks, packing checks up to once a year and a full overhaul every 5 to 10 years, with seat leakage tested to ANSI/FCI 70 2.

What Is Control Valve Maintenance?

Control valve maintenance is the planned inspection, adjustment, repair and testing of the valve body, trim, packing, actuator, positioner and air supply so the valve follows its signal and meets its shut off class. It combines routine checks in the field with workshop overhaul and diagnostic tests that show when a valve really needs attention.

Key Facts
  • Emerson says about half of plant maintenance is reactive, while predictive work is only 10 to 15 %
  • Emerson also notes that many valves scheduled for rebuild do not actually need it
  • Most field problems come from packing, the actuator diaphragm, the positioner and dirty instrument air
  • Seat leakage after overhaul is tested to ANSI/FCI 70 2 classes
  • A valve signature test checks friction, bench set and seat load without removing the valve

If you are new to the hardware, start with our guide to the basic parts of a control valve. Every task below maps to one of those parts, from the gland follower at the top to the seat ring at the bottom.

Advertisement

Preventive vs Predictive Control Valve Maintenance

Preventive work is time based, so a valve is pulled at every shutdown whether it needs it or not. Predictive work is condition based, using positioner diagnostics and signature tests to decide which valves to repair.

Preventive (Time Based)
  • Fixed intervals, simple to plan
  • Catches wear in severe service
  • Risk of rebuilding healthy valves
  • Reassembly errors can add new faults
Predictive (Condition Based)
  • Uses diagnostics from smart positioners
  • Repairs only valves that need it
  • Needs software and trained staff
  • Shortens shutdown work lists

Emerson writes that valves are frequently rebuilt regardless of actual condition, and that a diagnostic check before removal lets service be cancelled or postponed. Our article on predictive vs preventive maintenance covers the wider plant view, and this overview of types of maintenance explains reactive, preventive and condition based methods.

Do You Know?

Emerson states that in a typical plant predictive work is only 10 to 15 % of maintenance, while it should ideally be close to 50 %. Reactive work, about 50 % today, should ideally fall to 10 to 25 %.

How Do You Check a Control Valve?

A good control valve maintenance round needs only a torch, a soap solution and the DCS trend. Walk the valve from the air supply down to the body flanges and note anything that has changed since the last visit.

  • Packing gland: no weeping, no smoke on hot service, follower not bottomed out
  • Stem: clean, straight, no scoring or deposits above the gland
  • Actuator: no air leak at diaphragm case bolts, vent clear, spring case not corroded
  • Positioner: feedback arm tight, gauges readable, no hiss when steady
  • Air set: filter drained, supply pressure correct, no oil or water
  • Travel: DCS output and valve position agree within tolerance
  • Body and bonnet: no leaks at flanges, no unusual noise or vibration

Wet or oily air is a common hidden cause of sticking positioners, so read our notes on instrument air dew point risks. If travel and output disagree, our valve positioner troubleshooting guide lists the usual faults.

Quick Tip

Spray soap solution on positioner fittings, tubing and diaphragm case bolts with the valve at mid travel. Leaks only show while the actuator is pressurised, and a small hiss at a fitting can waste more air than the positioner bleed.

How to Adjust Valve Packing

Packing leaks are the most visible failure in control valve maintenance and the easiest to make worse. UNITEC D advises tightening gland nuts evenly in small increments, starting at 30 to 50 % of the OEM torque and cycling the stem between adjustments.

1
Check the type
Confirm PTFE or graphite packing and whether it is live loaded.
2
Stroke first
Cycle the valve to see if the leak stops as packing settles.
3
Tighten evenly
Take up both gland nuts by equal small amounts using a torque wrench.
4
Stroke again
Cycle the valve and watch the leak and the travel trend.
5
Check friction
Over tight packing causes stiction, so confirm smooth travel.
6
Repack if needed
If the follower is near bottom, replace the rings at the next window.

When repacking, UNITEC D says to cut rings at about 45 degrees and stagger each joint by 90 to 120 degrees. For low emission sets and live loading, see our guide on low emission control valve packing, and use stiction detection to prove the packing is not too tight.

Myth: Tighter packing is always safer
Fact: Over tight packing adds friction, causes stiction and makes the loop cycle
Myth: A rebuild at every shutdown is best practice
Fact: Emerson notes many valves pulled for rebuild did not need it
Myth: Bench set equals the spring range on the nameplate
Fact: Bench set is measured with no process load and must be checked against the specification
Myth: If the valve strokes, the positioner is fine
Fact: Smooth stroking can hide drift, air leaks and poor seat load

Trim Inspection, Lapping and Seat Leak Test

During a workshop overhaul the plug, seat ring, cage and stem are cleaned and inspected for erosion, galling and cavitation pitting. Our guide to control valve trim types helps you identify the parts, while cavitation and flashing explains why some trims wear so fast.

DisassembleRemove actuator, bonnet and trim, tagging every part.
Clean and inspectCheck plug, seat and guides for wear, cracks and pitting.
Lap metal seatsLap plug to seat with fine compound if the damage is light.
Replace partsFit new gaskets, packing and any worn trim.
ReassembleTorque bonnet bolts in a cross pattern to OEM values.
Seat testTest leakage against the specified class before dispatch.

Lapping only polishes small marks, so deeply cut or wire drawn seats need new trim. After overhaul, test to the class on the datasheet, explained in our article on control valve seat leakage classes.

ClassAllowed Leakage (ANSI/FCI 70 2)Test MediumTypical Use
II0.5 % of rated capacityAir or waterDouble port valves
III0.1 % of rated capacityAir or waterGeneral throttling
IV0.01 % of rated capacityAir or waterMetal seated globe valves
V0.0005 mL/min of water per inch of port per psiWaterTight metal seats
VIBubbles per minute by port sizeAir or nitrogenSoft seated valves

For Classes II to IV, UNITEC D gives a test pressure of 50 psi (3.4 bar) or the maximum operating differential, whichever is lower. If a valve still passes after overhaul, our list of control valve passing causes points to seat load and actuator problems.

Actuator, Diaphragm and Bench Set Check

Diaphragms harden and crack with age and heat, so they should be replaced at overhaul or whenever the case leaks. Our article on actuator bench set and spring range shows how to record the start and full travel pressures with no process load.

Then calibrate the positioner at 0, 25, 50, 75 and 100 % input, and UNITEC D suggests investigating any deviation above 2 % of full travel. Follow our valve positioner calibration procedure and record results as described in as found and as left records.

Quick Tip

Check stroking time after any actuator or positioner work, especially on shutdown valves. A new diaphragm or a changed tubing size can alter speed, as our page on control valve stroking time explains.

Valve Signature and Diagnostics

A valve signature plots actuator pressure against travel through a full stroke. Emerson says a full signature checks the response over the stroke, measures seating pressure and monitors actuator pressure and movement, all in one test.

Good control valve maintenance compares each new signature with the baseline taken at commissioning, which our guide on signature test diagnostics explains step by step. A growing hysteresis loop points to packing friction, while a shifted spring line points to a broken spring or wrong bench set.

The same trend data can feed analytics, as described in this guide to predictive maintenance with machine learning. For shutdown valves, partial stroke testing gives a similar health check without a trip.

How Often Should Control Valves Be Serviced?

There is no single interval for control valve maintenance, because service severity, criticality and diagnostics vary widely. UNITEC D suggests the starting points below, which you should adjust from your own failure history.

TaskSuggested Interval (UNITEC D)Typical Time
External visual inspectionMonthly or quarterly15 to 30 min
Packing adjustment and leak checkQuarterly to annually30 to 60 min
Actuator and positioner calibrationAnnually or every two years1 to 2 h
Full packing replacementEvery 3 to 5 years2 to 4 h
Seat leak testEvery 3 to 5 years or after trim change2 to 3 h
Full valve overhaulEvery 5 to 10 years4 to 8 h
Do You Know?

A positioner that bleeds air continuously costs money every hour of the year. The calculator below turns a measured leak rate into an annual energy cost so you can justify a repair.

Instrument Air Leak Cost Calculator
Annual Cost
Air lost 24000 m³ per year, energy 2880 kWh, cost about Rs 25920 per year
Solved example: 50 L/min leak
Air = 50 × 60 × 8000 ÷ 1000
Air = 24000 m³ per year
Energy = 24000 × 0.12 = 2880 kWh
Cost = 2880 × Rs 9 = Rs 25920 per year

Take the specific energy from your compressor data sheet, since 0.12 kWh per m³ is only an example. For the steady consumption of positioners and actuators, use our instrument air consumption calculator.

Spare Parts List for Control Valve Maintenance

Keep packing sets, gaskets, diaphragms and positioner spares in stock, plus full trim sets for critical valves. These parts cause most shutdown delays when they are missing.

Packing set
Rings, spacers and springs for each stem size and material.
Gasket kit
Bonnet and seat ring gaskets, never reused after opening.
Diaphragm
One per actuator size, stored away from heat and sunlight.
Trim set
Plug, seat ring and cage for critical or severe service valves.
Positioner spares
Feedback arm, relay and filter elements, or a complete spare unit.
Air set
Filter regulator and gauge for each common supply pressure.

Control Valve Maintenance Troubleshooting

Most valve faults trace back to packing, trim, the actuator diaphragm or instrument air quality. Use the table below to match each symptom with its likely cause and fix.

SymptomLikely CauseFix
Packing leakWorn or under torqued packingAdjust evenly, repack at next window
Valve sticks then jumpsOver tight packing or galled guideReduce gland load, inspect trim
Valve passes when closedDamaged seat or low seat loadLap or replace trim, check bench set
Slow or no strokeDiaphragm leak or blocked air supplyReplace diaphragm, drain air filter
Loop huntsPositioner tuning, stiction or deadbandRetune, check friction, see signature
Position driftsLoose feedback linkage or wet airTighten arm, fix air quality

For loop cycling, start with our guide on control valve hunting and oscillation, then use the wider control valve troubleshooting checklist.

Control Valve Maintenance FAQ

What is the difference between preventive and predictive control valve maintenance?

Preventive maintenance follows a fixed schedule, while predictive maintenance uses positioner diagnostics to repair only valves that need it. Emerson notes predictive work is only 10 to 15 percent of plant maintenance today, although it should be close to 50 percent.

Many valves pulled for rebuild on a schedule turn out to be healthy.

How do you check if a control valve is working properly in the field?

Compare the controller output with the valve position on the DCS trend at 0, 25, 50, 75 and 100 percent. Then check the valve for packing leaks, air leaks and unusual noise.

UNITEC D suggests investigating any travel deviation above 2 percent of full travel with a step test or signature.

How often should control valves be serviced in a typical process plant?

It depends on service severity and loop criticality, but UNITEC D suggests monthly or quarterly visual checks and packing checks up to once a year. Full overhaul is suggested every 5 to 10 years.

Erosive or cavitating service needs shorter intervals, so adjust the plan from your own failure records.

How do you stop a control valve packing leak without causing stiction?

First stroke the valve a few times, since new packing often settles and seals. If it still leaks, tighten both gland nuts evenly in small steps, starting at 30 to 50 percent of OEM torque as UNITEC D advises.

Stroke again after each step and watch the trend for stick slip.

How to calculate the yearly cost of an instrument air leak at a valve?

Multiply the leak rate in L/min by 60 and by operating hours, divide by 1000 for m³, then multiply by compressor specific energy and tariff. For example, 50 L/min for 8000 hours at 0.12 kWh per m³ and Rs 9 per kWh costs about Rs 25920 a year.

What is a valve signature test and what does it show?

A valve signature test strokes the valve slowly while recording actuator pressure against travel. It shows friction, spring range, bench set and available seat load, all without removing the valve.

A growing hysteresis loop compared with the commissioning baseline usually points to tight packing, a key finding in predictive control valve maintenance.
